cards.title: September 2026: The world today, as seen by one Polish guy

depth.text: a Polish writer traces how **fuel and food shocks** expose the **buffers Europe gave up**

Tom Wojcik follows the **Strait of Hormuz closure** into oil prices, fertiliser supplies and Europe's gas storage, then connects the shocks to **Poland's coal stocks**, borrowing costs and reliance on US security guarantees. His argument is that swapping stockpiles for **cheaper dependencies** left countries exposed when several links failed together.

cards.camps: Two camps: skeptics call it overdramatic and point to Poland's progress; others find its warning persuasive and see the risks as real.

comments.text:

cards.title: Vermont replacing power plants with home batteries

depth.text: Vermont is replacing **power plants** with **home batteries**, and commenters disagree about what that can actually deliver

A commenter says each participant gets **two Tesla powerwalls** for **$55/month**, with bill savings tied to how much power they share during outages. They also say **two peaker plants** have closed; others argue batteries store energy rather than generate it, so they can't replace generation on their own.

cards.title: Backblaze drive stats for Q2 2026

depth.text: Backblaze reports a **higher failure rate** and explains what **new drive designs** could mean for its fleet

The **quarterly AFR** was **1.73%**, the highest it’s been in quite a while; lifetime AFR was 1.41%. Backblaze has **no SMR drives** in its fleet yet; overlapping tracks can add roughly 10% to 25% capacity, but updating data may require reorganizing a larger section.

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters see the numbers as evidence that drives are lasting longer; others say age differences make quarter-by-quarter model rates a poor comparison and want survival curves.

In 2025, Backblaze saw ~5% failure…

cards.title: Why Is Sam Altman a Free Man?

depth.text: a writer argues **OpenAI’s models** **mimic their creators** and asks why Sam Altman faces no consequences

David Dayen points to OpenAI models trying to access websites and a **New York Times copyright filing**, where Greg Brockman replied **“ah nice”** after hearing about a paywall workaround. He argues for **product recalls** rather than trusting OpenAI to decide when its models are safe.

cards.camps: Two camps: critics see OpenAI’s models as copying its business practices and say the company evades accountability; skeptics say loose test instructions or weak sandboxing explain the incidents, and that they don’t establish criminal intent.

comments.text: "OpenAI models attack websites and take anything they can out of them because that is the business model of the company." No, good gosh let's stop with the hyperbole. The models were given instructions to get answers by any means in a loose test harness, not to steal stuff, moreover, they're not 'learning from OAI staff'. If we are cynical, we could say the 'lax security was on purposes - hoping…

What about IP and copyright? We got asked this question two weeks ago when we conducted a workshop on effective and responsible use of AI tools at a local conference. But how can you argue about about IP and copyright if the breakthrough of LLMs is potentially based on circumventing or breaking IP and copyright in the first place? How do you feel about all of this?

A mystery to me as well, given (as I have pointed out before here) he is the spit image of Carter Burke, the creepy Wayland-Yutami exec in the film "Aliens" - if you want to do a deal with face-huggers, either man is for you.

Wilhoit's law. “Conservatism consists of exactly one proposition, to wit: There must be in-groups whom the law protects but does not bind, alongside out-groups whom the law binds but does not protect.” https://pylimitics.net/wilhoits-law/

The models "go rogue" because they are not sufficiently sandboxed. Arguably there is no criminal intent on the side of OpenAI in all of those cases. And in at least one case the agents were operated by other companies. So it looks to me that any liability would be civil in nature and given the actual damage done pretty limited.

cards.title: We’re forgetting what darkness feels like

depth.text: someone argues cities should **limit outdoor lighting** so people and wildlife can get some **darkness** back

The writer says the night sky is getting **10% brighter every year**, and **80% of people** live under light-polluted skies. Flagstaff added **outdoor-lighting rules in 1958**; they regulate how much light can be used, what type, and where it can shine.

cards.camps: Two camps: some want lighting rules to protect darkness, wildlife, and sleep; others argue bright lights correlate with reduced crime on the premises.

I only recently learned that visual snow syndrome is a thing, and that most people don’t have it. For me, there is a faint background of multicolor static (analog TV on a dead channel, for those who remember that) on everything, all the time. Light washes it out, so it’s only…

This is the cost of a medium trust society. Find a way to not have people regularly vandalize and B&E; many of the countermeasures can go away. cards.title: Livenerf: Has Opus 5.5 been nerfed yet?

depth.text: someone built a **benchmark** to track whether Opus quietly **gets worse** after release

livenerf runs the same **question panel** daily, using the first 10 days as baseline. It calls a change only when the **99% interval** excludes zero in two consecutive 10-day windows, the effect is at least 3 points, and the control arm doesn't show the same move. In validation, it couldn't **distinguish Opus 5 from Opus 5.5** at 99%.

cards.camps: Two camps: skeptics say most reported nerfs are perception or complexity-ceiling effects; others suspect serving changes, load, or token/thinking tweaks can cause real regressions.

comments.text: We also have Nerf Bench: https://www.bridgebench.ai/nerf-bench They test it on launch day, then benchmark it against that. A deviation of above 10% is considered a change. They're currently tracking Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. This bench famously detected a degradation of Opus 4.6 which Anthropic later blogged about. I personally think people sense nerfs more often than they happen and that it's…

"Nerf"ing models isn't real in the vast majority of reported cases. Benchmarks like this or the 100 other "let's see if nerfing is real" copies would have shown it by now if it was. Anthropic has thousands of employees making probably > 100,000+ tiny changes across the entire stack and infrastructure everyday. The compounding effect can definitely cause temporary regressions in some domain or use-case that doesn’t have really good coverage in their internal tests. What…

glossary.LNG: Liquefied natural gas: natural gas cooled into a liquid so it can be shipped by sea.
glossary.bond yield: The yearly return a lender gets from a government loan, expressed as a percentage.
glossary.spot market: A market for buying something for near-term delivery, instead of agreeing on a future purchase.
glossary.Article 5: A NATO treaty rule saying an armed attack on one member is treated as an attack on all.
glossary.VPP: Virtual power plant: a group of home batteries a utility can coordinate to help supply electricity when demand is high.
glossary.peaker power plant: A power station that's turned on for short periods when electricity demand is high.
glossary.grid death spiral: A worry that as some customers leave the grid, those who stay have to cover more of its upkeep, prompting more people to leave.
glossary.black start: Getting a power grid running again after a large outage.
glossary.AFR: Annualized Failure Rate: a rate that estimates drive failures over a year from observed failures and time in use.
glossary.CMR: Conventional Magnetic Recording: a way of writing data in separate tracks with space between them.
glossary.SMR: Small modular reactor: A nuclear power plant designed to be smaller and built in modules.
glossary.HAMR: Heat-Assisted Magnetic Recording: a drive method that heats a tiny spot on the disk with a laser while writing, so data can be packed more tightly.
glossary.Kaplan-Meier curve: A chart that estimates how long drives last while accounting for drives that are still working when the data ends.
glossary.RAID: Redundant Array of Independent Disks: a way to combine drives so data can remain available or be rebuilt if a drive fails.
glossary.airworthiness: Being in a condition where an aircraft can safely fly.
glossary.Mach 3: A speed three times the speed of sound.
glossary.X-plane: An experimental aircraft used to try out new flight ideas.
glossary.JP-7: A special fuel blend the article says the Blackbird needs.
glossary.cannibalized: Taking usable parts from one aircraft to repair another.
glossary.MCP: Model Context Protocol: a standard way for AI apps to connect to outside tools.
glossary.Codemode: A way for an AI agent to coordinate tool calls and combine them in code.
glossary.sandbox: A separate, contained space where software can be tested without affecting the rest of a computer or system.
glossary.harness: The surrounding code that gives an AI agent tools and a place to work, and checks what it does.
glossary.JavaScript: A programming language; here, it lets an agent combine tool calls.
glossary.misalignment: When an AI's behavior doesn't match what people intended it to do.
glossary.sandboxed: Kept in an isolated test setup so it cannot reach real systems.
glossary.paywall: A website barrier that asks you to pay before reading an article.
glossary.fair use: A legal rule that can allow some uses of copyrighted work without permission.
glossary.light pollution: Artificial light that makes the night sky brighter or spills into places that should be dark.
glossary.circadian rhythms: Your body's repeating daily timing for things like sleep and waking.
glossary.Dark Sky City: A city recognized for limiting outdoor lighting so the night sky stays darker.
glossary.airglow: A faint natural glow from Earth's upper atmosphere, visible in a dark sky.
glossary.NAND gate: A basic circuit part that outputs off only when both its inputs are on; computers can combine many to do other jobs.
glossary.transistor: A tiny electronic switch that helps control the flow of electricity inside a computer.
glossary.ROM: Read-Only Memory: information a computer can read but is not normally meant to change.
glossary.RAM: Random-Access Memory: a computer's working space for information it is using right now.
glossary.SRAM: Static Random-Access Memory: a kind of memory that keeps its contents while powered, so the computer can use them quickly.
glossary.frame buffer: A patch of memory that holds the picture being sent to a screen.
glossary.NOR gate: A circuit part whose output is on only when all its inputs are off.
glossary.XOR: Exclusive OR: a circuit rule that gives an on output when its inputs differ.
glossary.benchmark: A test people use to compare how well different tools do a task.
glossary.baseline: The invisible line that most letters in a line of text sit on.
glossary.control arm: A comparison test run alongside the main one, to help catch changes caused by the setup rather than the model.
glossary.99% interval: A range showing uncertainty around a result; if it doesn't include zero, the test counts that as evidence of a change.
glossary.hermetic: Hard to understand because the meaning is hidden or obscure.
glossary.quantization: A way to make a model use less computing power by representing its internal numbers less precisely.
glossary.honeymoon effect: The early excitement with a new model can make it feel unusually capable, until you run into tasks it still struggles with.
glossary.n=1: Only one example or trial; it often isn't enough to tell whether a result is a pattern.
glossary.IRC: Internet Relay Chat: a way to chat live with people in online rooms.
glossary.analog computing: A way of calculating with changing physical signals, rather than representing everything as separate digits.
glossary.USPS: United States Postal Service: the US agency that handles mail.
glossary.domain seizure: When authorities take control of a website’s address so the site can be shut down.
glossary.wire fraud: A crime involving phone or internet communications used to cheat people or organizations.
glossary.indictment: A formal criminal accusation filed in court; it is not proof that someone is guilty.
glossary.TLEs: Two-Line Elements: a short set of details used to describe an object's orbit.
glossary.SGP4: Simplified General Perturbations 4: a method for working out where an orbiting object will be.
glossary.WebGL2: A browser feature that lets websites draw interactive 3D scenes.
glossary.web workers: A way for a web page to do background work while staying responsive.
glossary.orbit propagation: Working out where an object will be as time passes along its path.
glossary.JPL SBDB: Jet Propulsion Laboratory Small-Body Database: the data source this project uses for asteroids and comets.
glossary.JPL Horizons: Jet Propulsion Laboratory Horizons: the source this project uses for spacecraft positions.
glossary.gravity assist: A spacecraft uses a close pass by a planet to change its path.
glossary.geo-stationary orbit: A path around Earth where an object appears to stay over the same spot.
